# ICP for search: what was studied

This is the research behind the ICP words of the pack: what an ICP is, how it differs from a segment, a buying
group, a persona and qualification, which fields earn a place in a search, and which numbers to stop repeating.
It feeds the linkedin-outreach-method skill (its ICP reference) and the linkedin-personas skill (the words at
the top of the persona card). Every claim with its strength is in `evidence.md`; every link, read or not, is in
`sources.md`. The sister folder `personas/` covers what a persona card holds; this one covers the company half
and the boundary between the two.

Written 2026-10-30 from the pack and the product read for ambiguity, and two web passes (ICP
frameworks, persona and buying-role sources). Where a point was re-checked live that day, `sources.md` says so.

## Why this exists

An audit found the ICP and persona words imprecise: the pack used "ICP" for companies only, while the product's
search plan holds an ICP together with its roles, and "target", "group", "fit", "signal" and "card" each had three
to five meanings across the skills (section 10 settles them). The fix keeps the pack's meaning and explains the product's shape:
**an ICP is the company half of a plan segment; a plan group is the searchable half of a persona.**


## The short answer

- **ICP, buying group, persona and qualification are four different units.** A company, the people in it with a
  say in one purchase, a role in a situation, and one deal. Only the first and the searchable half of the third
  can be read before talking to anyone.
- **One ICP is a set of companies that get about the same value and are reached the same way** (Fuentes). If it
  cannot be written as a query, it is a description of a segment, not an ICP.
- **Every field narrows, geometrically.** At 9 or more attributes, even the best 1% of descriptions matched
  nobody in 5 of 6 real datasets (Chapman et al. 2008). Read what the whole plan returns, never a per-field count.
- **Timing is not fit.** Fit decides who is in; timing decides the order. Signals, triggers and Why now belong
  to ordering and to the opener.
- **An ICP gives control over the list. Nobody has shown it raises replies.** No randomised comparison of a
  broad against a narrow outbound list exists anywhere.

## 1. The layers

| Layer | Unit | Question it answers | Changes about every | Knowable before contact |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Market | All companies that could ever buy | Where could we play at all | Years | Yes |
| Segment | A group of companies the market splits into | Which groups exist | Years | Yes |
| ICP | One kind of company | Is this company worth reaching (fit, not timing) | Quarters | Yes: this is what defines it |
| Buying group | The people in one company with a say in one purchase | Who decides, for this need | Per purchase | Partly, and only by asking |
| Buying role | What one person does in that purchase | Uses it, chooses it, signs, can veto, gets blamed | Per purchase | Rarely |
| Persona, targeting half | One person, by role | Who to find: titles, function, seniority | Quarters | Yes: a profile shows it |
| Persona, messaging half | One person, by situation | What to say: trigger, priorities, barriers, words | Quarters | No: learned from the user and from replies |
| Qualification (BANT, MEDDIC, SPICED) | One deal | Is this deal real now, worth a seller's hours | Days | No: needs a conversation |

The axis under the table: an ICP is a property of a company and holds whether or not a deal exists;
qualification is a property of a deal. Kellogg puts it most plainly: "Should an ICP include sales qualification
criteria? No." MEDDIC's own site calls it a framework for qualifying "opportunities" (created at PTC in 1996).
No peer-reviewed or randomised evaluation exists for BANT, MEDDIC, MEDDPICC, CHAMP or SPICED.

In the pack's words, after the 2026-10-30 decision:

- **ICP** = the kind of company worth reaching (trade, size, place, at most one situation a company page shows).
  In the search plan it is the company half of one segment.
- **Segment** = one ICP as the plan holds it, with its roles (groups) attached. Plan order is priority.
- **Plan group** = one job searched in one segment, with its title variants: the searchable half of a persona.
- **Persona** = a role in a situation inside one ICP's companies. Its card holds Found by (searchable, copied
  from plan groups) and the message half (Why now, Pain, Objection, Proof, Offer: never searchable).
- **Buying group** = never a filter; it fills the card's "Who else decides".
- **Qualification** = never a filter; no profile shows it.

## 2. Working definition: same value, same reach

> "An ICP must be a single market segment: a group of people for whom the value of solving a problem is roughly
> the same, and who can be reached in roughly the same way." Jake Fuentes, via Lenny's Newsletter (Practice)

Two tests, both usable: value homogeneity and reach homogeneity. A set that fails either is several ICPs. The
cheapest form of the value test is the pitch: if part of the group needs the pitch rewritten, it is two ICPs.

**Basis against descriptor** (Choffray and Lilien 1980, p. 331, read in full). A basis is the reason companies
belong together (they react the same way to the offer). A descriptor is an observable variable that predicts
membership (industry, headcount, country). Every field on an ICP form is a descriptor; the form never asks for the
basis. That is why a message written from a filter list comes out bland: the reason is missing. The same paper
states the three conditions a usable segment must pass: homogeneous response, large enough to be worth it
(parsimony), and describable by observable variables (accessibility). A search can measure two of them: the count
is parsimony, and whether the search can run the definition is accessibility. Homogeneity only shows in replies.

**Two stages, in order.** Wind and Cardozo (1974): macro-segmentation on the organisation, then
micro-segmentation on the decision-making unit inside it. The primary is paywalled and unread; the two stages are
confirmed through Choffray and Lilien (1980, p. 332): the macro stage runs on "secondary sources". So a field
public data can answer is a legitimate ICP field, and a field only a conversation reveals belongs to the person
stage or to qualification. The stopping rule (go to the person level only when one message to one list draws
clearly different responses from different kinds of people) is weakly sourced: it reaches us through a bachelor
thesis quoting Wind and Cardozo.

## 3. The four-part field test

A field stays in an ICP only if all four hold (after Mora Cortez et al. 2021 and Kotler's segment criteria):

1. **Observable without contact.** A company page, a profile or public data shows it (Bonoma and Shapiro's outer
   nests).
2. **Discriminating.** Companies differ on it, and the difference tracks an outcome.
3. **Actionable.** Some later decision branches on its value (who is searched, which card, which opener).
4. **Filterable.** It can be written as a query, not as prose.

The one-sentence test: if you cannot say in one sentence what you would do differently for a company on either
side of the field, delete it.

**A label is not a capability.** A 5,000-account list filtered on an industry label got 1% replies; rebuilt on the
capability the product actually required, it became 800 accounts and 27% replies. The source is the agency that did
the work (Practice): keep the mechanism, not the numbers. The label sounded like the customer; the capability is
the customer.

**Fields to delete:**

- revenue band for private companies (not observable, mostly estimated);
- budget, authority, timeline, "actively evaluating" (qualification smuggled in);
- free-text pain paragraphs (not filterable; they belong on the persona card);
- psychographics;
- persona demographics (age, tenure, education);
- an industry label used where a capability is meant;
- band edges no decision depends on.

**Measured strikes against common fields:**

- **Adoption stage.** Per-period profitability was highest for the early majority, not innovators; and the same
  company can be an early adopter of one technology and a late adopter of another (Gartner's own ETA document).
- **Company size as a predictor of who is in the room: contested.** A census study (31 firms, 62 purchases, 241
  interviews) found size changed no dimension of the buying centre; Pedeliento et al. 2019 found size "clearly
  determines" end-user involvement. The 2023 review (Cabanelas, Mora Cortez and Charterina, IMM 108, 89 articles)
  calls for more research.
- **Industry** is a stand-in for needs, not their cause.

## 4. The arithmetic floor, and the field count reconciled

Chapman, Love, Milham, ElRif and Alford 2008 (HFES 52nd annual meeting, pp. 1107-1111), read in full:

- A profile is a conjunction of attributes, so the share of people it matches falls geometrically with each one.
- Six real survey datasets (N = 268 to 10,307), 10,000 random descriptions each.
- At the 99th percentile, descriptions with 9 or more attributes matched nobody in 5 of 6 datasets. Only one
  dataset (the IT one) had a 7-plus attribute description matching more than 0.3% of people.
- Observed against predicted prevalence: r = 0.394 to 0.713 on the survey datasets (0.857 to 0.869 on simulated
  data).
- Limits, stated by the authors: the descriptions were random, 5 of 6 datasets are consumer, and the paper "does
  not address the utility of personas".

**The numbers that float around, and how they fit:**

| Number | Where it comes from | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 9 or more attributes match nobody; 7 or more pass 0.3% in one dataset only | Chapman et al. 2008 | Measured ceiling of a conjunction |
| "About five" fields or personas | Miller-Heiman "top five", ITSMA "three or fewer personas", Goodwin's merge rule | An unmeasured meeting point of three practitioner traditions |

**Working answer: read the whole plan's count, never a per-field count.** A search returns a count, so every added
attribute shows what it costs on screen. That is the one thing a search adds to Chapman's arithmetic.

Related: Dolnicar, Grün, Leisch and Schmidt (2014), simulation, 70 to 100 data points per segmentation variable for
data-driven segmentation. Most ICPs are not found in data at all; they are chosen by people ("constructive
segmentation"). Chapman and Milham 2006: a persona cannot be falsified.

## 5. Buying groups

- **No constant.** Published sizes run from about 5 to over 20 (4.8 to 23 across published counts). The counting
  rule decides the number: buyer surveys give the smallest groups, seller surveys larger, CRM data the largest. The
  same firm publishes 6 to 10 in one report and 13 to 15 or 14 to 23 in others. "Median 6 to 10" is an unsourced
  sentence inside its own Gartner/CEB document. The Clari 7 to 19 range comes from closed-won deals only.
  Forrester's "94% with four or more" is published as three or more.
- **Roles, not a number.** Users, influencers, buyers, deciders, gatekeepers: Webster and Wind 1972 (Journal of
  Marketing 36(2), 12-19). A conceptual model, never tested as a partition; the five-role list reaches us through
  textbooks. What to ship instead of a number: who uses it, who chooses it, who signs, who can veto, who gets
  blamed.
- **Ask, don't infer.** Choffray and Lilien 1980 predicted a firm's buying-group make-up from the firm's own
  characteristics 47% of the time against 27% by chance (118 firms, one product category). Inside one account
  segment, four micro-segments (12%, 31%, 32%, 25%) differed in which functions took part. So the person definition
  is a set of roles, and who to talk to inside a company is asked of the user, not read off the company's facts.
- **The sign of the group-relevance finding, and only the sign.** Gartner 2025 (n = 632 buyers, press release of 7
  May 2025): buying-group relevance makes a high-quality deal 3 times more likely; individual relevance has a "59%
  negative impact" on consensus. The "+20%" figure for collective learning is CEB 2015 (The Challenger Customer),
  not Gartner. All of it is self-reported, measured
  inside active purchases rather than at a cold first touch, and relative with no base. The usable test: a message
  the reader can forward against one that only flatters them.
- **Direction of group size: contested.** CEB 2015 says bigger groups lower purchase likelihood; Gartner 2020 says
  more functions mean more high-quality deals; Forrester 2026 says 94% of groups of six or more report benefits.
  None has a control.
- **The private job.** Romaniuk 2022: every B2B reader has two jobs, the company's and their own (promotion, not
  being blamed).

## 6. The case against narrow targeting, and what it actually measured

- **Neither school measured an outbound list.** All five Ehrenberg-Bass B2B reports were searched for ABM, prospect
  list and outbound: zero hits. All 435 cases in Binet and Field's B2B work are advertising award entries. Nobody can
  cite them against a filtered outbound list, and nobody can cite them for one.
- **"Narrow targeting is counterproductive" is narrower than it sounds.** In the institute's report it rests on one
  unread textbook chapter. Sharp objects to "restrictive" and "skewed" targeting but endorses "tailoring". Dawes:
  "sure, do some targeting for people who are ready to buy, but if that's all you do..."
- **The other side prescribes tight targeting.** The B2B Effectiveness Code (Binet and Field) puts about 54% of budget
  on activation "targeted tightly at your most likely buyers today" (fewer than 50 cases; their own caveat: "should
  not be followed too precisely").
- **Pauwels' boundary.** Broad reach wins when acquisition is cheap and lifetime value barely varies. B2B is the
  reverse. Pauwels and Koll 2022 (153 brands, consumer goods) found small brands in growing markets benefit from
  differentiation.
- **The randomised targeting evidence** (none of it B2B outbound): Simester et al. 2020, one of seven targeting
  methods beat treating everyone the same; Ascarza 2018, targeting the most responsive beat targeting the highest
  risk; Athey et al. 2024, targeting half the population captured about 75% of the benefit; Neumann, Tucker and
  Whitfield 2019, bought audience attributes improved on random selection by 0 to 77%. What it supports: a filter
  saves budget at a known cost in results. It does not buy better replies.
- **The claim the argument rests on is unread.** "Competing brands' user profiles hardly differ" has three primaries
  (Kennedy, Ehrenberg and Long 2000; Uncles et al. 2012; Anesbury et al. 2017), all paywalled and none opened, and
  it was never tested on B2B firmographics.
- **Conflict of interest.** LinkedIn's B2B Institute commissioned most of both series; the institute publishes an
  independence policy.
- **Where fit does show up** (choosing different accounts gives different money; writing an ICP document was never
  shown to cause better choosing): Mutiny tier A 30%, tier B 8% lead to opportunity (one company); SaaS Capital
  retention by contract value (n over 1,500); ICONIQ, about 16 points higher retention for mid-market to enterprise
  sellers; Garland 2002, a third of customers produced 98% of profit; Venkatesan and Kumar 2004, choosing by
  lifetime value gave $143k against $71k profit in a holdout.
- **What an ICP cannot fix.** In 2.5M recorded B2B sales calls, 40 to 60% of deals end in no decision; of those, 44%
  are status quo and 56% indecision.

## 7. The circularity trap

- **Defining segments by outcome is a tautology.** Mora Cortez, Højbjerg Clarke and Freytag 2021 (Journal of
  Business Research 126, 415-428, 88 papers from 1986 to 2019): using performance as a segmentation variable creates
  "a tautological situation". A field must be an antecedent (industry, headcount, tech stack, business model,
  problem). Contract value, retention, lifetime value and fit scores are consequents: they can validate an ICP, never
  be fields in it.
- **Survivorship.** Won deals come from the companies the current ICP sent you to. An ICP re-derived from them
  reproduces itself and is silent about every segment never called. Kellogg: "your ICP starts out as an aspiration
  and becomes a regression". Expanding it means sampling outside it on purpose.
- **Loss data is mostly wrong.** Clozd, 1,000 deals: CRM loss reasons matched the buyer's own account 15% of the
  time; competitor tags were wrong in about 7 of 10; 44% of recorded reasons are outcomes ("went dark"), not reasons
  (Measured vendor: Clozd sells win-loss interviews, but states sample and method).
- **Usage data describes the product built before the ICP was known.** Jordan Woods, via OpenView (Practice). The
  remedy: interview non-customers about the problem, never about the product.
- **Churn.** Only product misalignment may update the ICP; a deal lost on price or execution may not (a16z,
  assertion).
- **The founding artefact already has the trap.** Miller and Heiman's Ideal Customer Profile (The New Strategic
  Selling, seen only through a third-party outline) is a five-criterion rubric built by contrasting best and worst
  customers.
- **Inside BeReach, at the scale of one person:** what someone kept or removed may reorder or shorten their roles;
  it may never invent a job, a kind of company or a place, and no ICP is inferred from people the person did not
  choose.

## 8. Timing is not fit

- **Membership against order.** Fit decides who is in; timing decides the order. A triggered company that fails fit
  is still a bad company. A fitting company with no trigger is one you contact later. The pack's words: Why now
  (the kind of moment, on the card), trigger (the event in the world), signal (the dated public fact that shows it),
  `whyNow` (one dated reason on one row). None of them is a plan field.
- **The 95:5 rule is a formula, not a measurement.** Dawes (Ehrenberg-Bass, 2021): one supplier change every five
  years gives 20% a year, about 5% a quarter. No dataset; Dawes calls it "a heuristic". Forrester (Arnold, 2025):
  "5% is too low on average across all B2B purchases". The usable part: ask how often the buyer buys X and derive
  the in-market share (two years between purchases gives about 13% a quarter). Dawes uses it to argue for broad
  reach; intent vendors cite it for the opposite.
- **"95% of the time the winner was on the Day One shortlist."** The same report has buyers evaluating 5.1 vendors
  with 3.6 on that list; a random winner lands on it about 71% of the time. Contested.
- **No controls in timing data.** About 20 vendor sources: no A/B test, holdout or matched control. Each compares a
  warm, self-selected group with cold strangers.
- **Public triggers erode.** One viral post brought 70 connection requests and 10 missed cold calls in a day (one
  operator). Quiet or lagged triggers beat loud ones; the trade is predictive power against durability.
- **Intent** (signs a company researches the problem) is a third axis. The pack's tools do not read it. The intent
  precision figures in circulation (92%, 87%, 81%) are repeated by affiliate sites with no method.

## 9. Title noise

One role is never one exact title. Five reasons:

- **Function and seniority are guessed by the platform** from the free-text title. Vendor guides warn they are
  wrong often enough not to use them alone (Vendor claim). Use them as loose checks.
- **People edit past titles.** Stanford with Revelio Labs (blog of 29 September 2026, re-read 2026-10-30): "nearly
  20% of established US LinkedIn users edited the titles or descriptions of jobs they had already left"; among tech
  workers nearly one in three. Sample and method are not shown on the page.
- **Title inflation and flat titles.** Datapeople reports a 38% rise in senior-sounding titles (Vendor claim). Some
  AI labs give everyone the same title ("member of technical staff"), so the title confers no seniority
  (observation via HC Mag). Indeed's "nearly 80% believe title inflation is common" is a Survey.
- **Self-chosen titles.** Grant, Berg and Cable, "Job titles as identity badges", Academy of Management Journal
  57(4), 2014, pp. 1201-1225 (field studies). Explains free-text titles that map to no function.
- **Normalisation research.** Decorte et al., "JobBERT: Understanding Job Titles through Skills", arXiv 2109.09605,
  2021: titles normalised through co-occurring skills, public benchmark (Measured). Large title taxonomies exist
  (a 30,000-entry platform taxonomy cited by one paper; Lightcast normalises 20M+ raw titles to 75,000+).

For search: one role is a set of title variants (spellings, short forms, languages, inflated forms) in each
market's languages and English, with function and seniority as loose checks. The persona is defined by the job the
person does; titles are only the evidence for it. Goodwin: one title can hold two personas, one persona can span
many titles.

## 10. The words, settled


**The product's own shape, as the pack now explains it:** segments = ICPs; groups = roles (one job each, with title
variants); plan order = priority; `icp` in an edit = a segment id. The plan has no signal, why-now, pain or
situation field. Memory types are `user-profile`, `offering`, `playbook`, plus a legacy `icp` that can be removed.


**Two pack texts reconciled.** "A full persona is the wrong ask" (from ITSMA's tiers) holds for choosing who to
find (that is a role filter), and a short, provisional, role-level card is right for writing (`../personas/README.md`,
The short answer).

**Is the role part of the ICP?** Kellogg says yes (one of four ICP elements); Gong, ITSMA and Wind and Cardozo say
no. The pack's answer is a shape, not a vote: the role is not part of the ICP, but the plan carries the roles on the
segment, so the two travel together in the search and separate on the card.

## 11. Frameworks, with their authors

- **Wind and Cardozo (Industrial Marketing Management 3(3), 1974).** Macro then micro segmentation. Primary unread;
  confirmed through Choffray and Lilien 1980. Practice, never tested.
- **Bonoma and Shapiro (MSI working paper 1983; HBR, May 1984; Segmenting the Industrial Market, Lexington Books).**
  Five nests, outside in: demographics; operating variables; purchasing approaches; situational factors; personal
  characteristics. Nests 1 and 2 can be searched on a profile or company page; nests 3 to 5 need contact. Known
  critique: the borders are blurred (Webster). Practice; HBR abstract and date only.
- **Geoffrey Moore (Crossing the Chasm, 1991).** One beachhead, then the next pin (the bowling alley); target-customer
  scenarios; "target customer, not target market". For search: widening is a deliberate move to an adjacent pin, not
  a looser filter. Practice; primary unread.
- **April Dunford (Obviously Awesome, 2019; Sales Pitch, 2023).** Best-fit customers "care a lot about your unique
  value"; segment after naming differentiated value. A filter must be a visible trait that predicts caring. Practice.
- **Aaron Ross and Marylou Tyler (Predictable Revenue, 2011).** The ICP is step one of Cold Calling 2.0. The exact
  checklist fields are untraced (summaries only). Practice.
- **Winning by Design (ICP blueprint PDF, 2022).** SPICED diagnosis, a quantitative firmographic pass, a qualitative
  pass with 5 to 10 customers, an ICP summary and 3 to 5 segment profiles. Its own caveat: past wins "may not be
  exactly the same as the ones you want to close in the future". It places Critical Event (timing) inside the ICP,
  which the pack does not. Its figure 2 rates are illustrative. Practice.
- **ITSMA tiers (Bev Burgess, from about 2003).** Strategic one-to-one, ABM Lite one-to-few, Programmatic one-to-many.
  A list of hundreds is one-to-many, so the ICP must be filters, not named accounts. Account counts per tier are
  untraced. Practice.
- **Tomasz Tunguz (blog, 10 February 2017).** "The hidden costs of non-ICP customers are real": roadmap pull,
  diluted message, support cost, churn; changing the ICP must be deliberate. No data (re-read 2026-10-30): a cost
  guard, not a proven win-rate lever. Counter: Jason Lemkin, complaints do not predict churn.
- **Ehrenberg-Bass (Sharp, How Brands Grow, 2010; Romaniuk's category entry points; Dawes, 95:5, 2021).** B2B double
  jeopardy (Romaniuk, Dawes and Faghidno 2021, Measured). Argues against one narrow search being the only motion, not
  against filtering. See sections 6 and 8.
- **Dave Kellogg (kellblog, 2025).** The ICP as aspiration that becomes a regression; the role as one of four ICP
  elements; bullseye rings; "faux focus". Practice.
- **Pruitt and Grudin (DUX 2003).** Personas built from "large sample market segmentation studies", segments chosen
  by market size and revenue, 3 to 6 personas, one anti-persona; "We have not tried to formally measure the impact".
  The clearest written link from segment to persona. Practice.
- **Adele Revella (The Buyer Persona Manifesto, 2016).** The profile is "the person you need to reach"; the 5 Rings
  are "the buying decision you need to influence": the two halves of a persona, named by one author. Practice.
- **Tony Zambito (from 2001 or 2002, date uncertain).** Buyer personas as how buyers decide; profiles as
  demographics. Practice.
- **ITSMA's role-based profile.** A profile from second-hand data "merely describe[s] who the buyer is"; a buyer
  persona describes the buying process (reached through a Momentum ITSMA 2021 summary; the 2017 post was not
  found). So a search knows who people are, not how they buy.
- **SiriusDecisions demand waterfall (Forrester blog, 17 May 2017).** The demand unit is a buying group organised
  around a need; a persona is only the engaged-stage test ("at least one contact who fits a designated buyer
  persona"). The original waterfall's year (2002 or 2006) is disputed. Practice.
- **Jobs to be done and Gothelf (Christensen et al., HBR 2016; Moesta and Spiek's four forces; Gothelf blog, 12 June
  2017).** The job replaces the descriptive part of a persona with the causal part (struggle, trigger); it does not
  replace the role filter used to find people. Gothelf: different personas can share one job; "no reason for them to
  be in conflict". Practice.

## 12. Do not repeat

**Six tells that a number has been laundered:**

1. a reduction over 100%;
2. a relative change with no base;
3. a confidence question reported as accuracy;
4. a base that is a hidden fraction of the sample;
5. an open top bucket quoted as a point ("31% at six" when the bucket is "six or more");
6. a live URL treated as proof (any path on that host returns 200).

**Folklore list**:

- "A strong ICP gives 68% higher win rates": TOPO 2019, 164 self-selected respondents, a confidence question
  reported as accuracy.
- "A tight ICP gives 25 to 30% better marketing ROI": no originator.
- "95% of buyers are not in market" as a measurement: a formula (section 8).
- "Buying group of 6 to 10": unsourced in its own document.
- "Signal-based selling gets 25 to 40% replies against 2 to 5% cold": traces to content farms.
- "Trigger events win 74% of the time" and "10x more likely to switch": untraced.
- "Knowing who not to sell to is as valuable as who to sell to": no evidence anywhere.
- "BANT invented by IBM in 1959": no primary; the one primary artefact is an IBM partner form from 2011.
- "57%, 67%, 80% of the journey done before contacting sales": 22 organisations in 2011; the 67% version was
  withdrawn by the firm that popularised it.
- "Three to seven personas": one 2002 case study.
- "Companies beating goals are 2x more likely to have personas": Cintell 2016, n = 137, self-selected.
- Revella's "half as many personas": her claim, no data.
- The ABM ROI series and "171% lift over matched controls" (the latter fabricated by a search summary in this
  project's own research tooling).
- Intent precision figures (92%, 87%, 81%): no method.
- Ross's exact ICP checklist fields; the origin of TAM, SAM and SOM: untraced.

## 13. Open questions

- Do attribute-based definitions discriminate in B2B on firmographics? The profile-sameness finding was never
  tested there.
- Does a broad or a narrow outbound list win? No randomised comparison exists; a user's own split test is the only
  way.
- What do managers actually use to judge an account high-value? (IMM 133, paywalled.)
- Primaries never read: Wind and Cardozo 1974, Shapiro and Bonoma 1984, Moore chapter 4, the Predictable Revenue ICP
  chapter, Miller-Heiman, Cooper 1999's section body, Christensen 2016's full text, the three "profiles hardly differ"
  papers, Kalafatis and Cheston 1997. Several Practice rows rest on secondary sources (`sources.md`).

## The honest promise

An ICP gives control over who is on the list and what a search costs. It is not shown to raise replies. Say so.
